So I've got a Trek 4300 series Mt bike with road tires on it currently, all of my riding is either sidewalk on major roads, or on the road through neighborhoods, just wondering what y'alls input is on investing in a road bike, not a super lightweight tri bike or anything, but i have seen some really nice road bikes on craigslist and whatnot, what do you all think?

My first advice to you is to stay off the sidewalk and learn how to ride your bike with the flow of traffic. Sidewalk riding is something you should only do in rare cases. You don't ordinarily belong there, and it's a great way to 1) piss off pedestrians, 2) collide with pedestrians, and 3) get hit by a car pulling out of a business or residential driveway. You should also avoid riding in the crosswalks at intersections. Look up videos on youtube to teach yourself how to ride in the road, and check your local DMV or similar for a manual that you can pick up to learn your local laws.

Secondly, I find that mountain bikes with road slicks are generally great for commuting as long as speed is NOT a concern. If you're in shape, then you can often pass people on road bikes who aren't in as good of a condition as you are, especially up a hill, but the gearing and the wider tires of a mountain bike are not made for speed. The gearing on a mountain bike is made for climbing, and the rims are made to take wider tires for safer descending over rough terrain.

A road bike will have rims that can take skinnier tires. While the 26 inch rims of a mtn bike like the trek 4300 will allow quicker acceleration from a stop, the larger diameter and skinnier width of your average 700c road bike tires are easily going to be faster over any real distance. A road bike will also destroy your mtn bike on a flat road or on a descent because the outer front chain ring has more teeth, allowing a strong rider to continue gaining speed while the comparatively fewer teeth of a mountain bike's outer ring wouldn't allow you to exert enough force to keep up without requiring you to be able to spin your legs faster than an airplane propeller.

The major trade-off is that narrower tires provide less cushion when the road is bumpy, so the ride will feel rougher.

In short, if you're in shape and you want to get around quickly, you should invest in a road bike. If not, then a mountain bike with slicks will do quite well.

I started commuting on a mtb like you. Then I bought a cheap road bike to try. I fell in love with the drop bars, but found that I preferred a more upright position like a mountain bike, and I liked the softer feel of 26 inch 1.75 wide tires. Plus I like using slime tubes, and they're very easy to get in that size almost anywhere. 26 inch tires and tubes in general can be found basically anywhere in the world.

I'm also into comfort over speed, especially since I end up doing most of my shopping on the bike, so I end up hauling a lot of extra weight. A steel frame bike is heavy, but it's softer because the steel flexes. Steel can also be repaired much more easily than carbon or aluminum.

All of this led me to settle on a surly long haul trucker with 26 inch rims as my primary bike.

Everyone will have different tastes. Personally, I think everyone should have at least 3 different bikes for different types of riding. But if you can only have one bike, you can't really go wrong with a sturdy mountain bike. It's going to be gentler on you and more durable, so you can ride it in all weather conditions all year. Road bikes aren't really good for winter riding.

Also, many shocks can be locked. You might try locking your shocks before you consider replacing the fork.

Eventually, you're probably going to want to just build your own bike with the exact components you like, so in my opinion, you should probably keep your costs as low as possible for now until you figure out what that is.
